  "factor_matrix": {
    "entry_documents": {"exposure": "Federal 2025 order: M/F-only markers, no X; Feb 2025 cable tells officers to refuse where document discrepancy casts reasonable doubt on sex and to consider fraud-based lifetime ineligibility for wilful misrepresentation; travellers report passports blocked/confiscated and being stranded; multiple foreign advisories issued.", "protection": "State IDs/birth certificates issue X markers and allow no-surgery gender change (resident-facing climate only); existing X passports valid to expiration; litigation pending and some orders enjoined.", "interaction": "State X markers cannot override federal visa/passport adjudication; a document mismatch discovered at the federal desk triggers the federal refusal and fraud analysis regardless of state protection.", "status": "documented"},
    "investigation_detention_custody": {"exposure": "Immigration custody: transgender men report forced-labour programmes, beatings, solitary confinement for refusal, and severe sexual abuse; federal corrections adopted conversion-therapy-style policy (hair cutting, hormone removal) from 2026 and stopped counting trans prisoners.", "protection": "Federal courts have blocked or enjoined several orders; habeas and litigation remain available in a functioning federal judiciary.", "interaction": "A visitor refused entry or held for document doubt enters this federal custody system, where state protections do not reach; state remedies cannot compel federal release.", "status": "documented"},
    "federal_state_facilities": {"exposure": "Federal order bars trans people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with identity (federal buildings, likely airports/courthouses); facility bans in a growing set of state/provinces, 4 with criminal triggers; one documented 2025 arrest of a trans woman (held 24h in men's ward).", "protection": "The division has no facility ban and mandates gender-neutral single-occupancy restrooms since 2019; sits in the 15-member 'Most Protective' tier (July 2026).", "interaction": "Within the division everyday facilities are safe, but federally owned or funded sites inside it follow the federal exclusion, so exposure persists at airports and federal buildings.", "status": "documented"},
    "care_services": {"exposure": "Federal rule moves to exclude under-18 coverage; DOJ subpoenaed under-19 patient records from 20+ hospitals in 2025; national crisis-lifeline LGBTQ services shut down.", "protection": "State 2023 statute codifies gender-affirming care on request including for interstate travellers; shield law (2023) protects patients/providers from out-of-jurisdiction charges; state maintained Medicaid coverage using federal funds in 2026.", "interaction": "Shield status protects a visitor from a ban home jurisdiction, but whether the 'on request' standard covers non-resident minors and what documentation a visiting minor needs is not_documented.", "status": "documented"},
    "threat_framing_law_enforcement": {"exposure": "Federal rhetoric: 'radical gender ideology' in counterterrorism framing, May 2026 strategy prioritizing 'radically pro-transgender' groups, orders describing minor care as 'mutilation'; reward scheme language creates chilling ambiguity, though ideology is never a reward criterion; 66% public support for birth-sex document rules.", "protection": "Division hate-crime law covers gender identity since 2003; trans panic defence repealed 2022; non-discrimination statute enforced upheld unanimously by state supreme court; 2017/2018 polling showed 64-73% support for LGBTQ protections; Indigenous four-gender traditions noted.", "interaction": "State law enforcement recasts hostility as protection, but a federal investigation or stop invokes the hostile federal posture; friction between levels creates unpredictability.", "status": "documented"},

  "synthesis": "Two sovereigns operate on one journey. The border and any federal facility are governed by a 2025 binary-sex regime: M/F-only markers, refusal where documents cast doubt on sex, a possible lifetime fraud finding, documented abuse in immigration custody, federal single-sex facility exclusion, and conversion-therapy-style practice in federal prisons — a universal document exposure with a severe custody tail. }","refusal":null,"reasoning":"We need to rate a combined regime: a highly protective US state within a hostile federal regime (traveler uses home passport — for an international trans traveler, federal passport/visa rules apply; entry screening cable with case-note tags, refusal where doubt on sex; detention in immigration custody with documented abuse for trans men).

Key traveler-facing exposures at federal level: passport marker restrictions (only M/F per assigned sex), visa adjudication refusal for document discrepancy / suspected misrepresentation → potential lifetime ineligibility for fraud; entry screening; immigration custody abuse documented (forced labor, beatings, sexual abuse of transgender men); federal facility ban in government-funded single-sex facilities (federal buildings, airports?); federal prisons conversion-therapy policy — applies to federal custody.

State protections: public accommodations discrimination ban covering hotels, restaurants, shops; shield law for care; hate crime law; no bathroom ban at state level; single-occupancy gender-neutral restrooms; X markers on state IDs; "Most Protective" tier.

Combined-regime: federal entry/document regime reaches every international visitor. Severity: denial of entry, fraud finding (lifetime bar), detention conditions documented as abusive. That's tier 2/state-tolerated targeting (immigration custody abuse) plus universal-exposure at border (document mismatch → doubt → refusal). No criminalisation of trans identity; no imprisonment for being trans at state level. Rule of law functioning at state level; federal courts partially blocking orders but Supreme Court allowed passport restrictions.

Score: contrast with anchors. 0.55-B: extended secondary screening, refused admission, administrative penalties — similar-ish but this dossier has documented immigration custody abuse (beatings, sexual abuse, solitary) which is severity 4-5 for those detained. However detention of trans travelers in immigration custody is not universal — most enter with proper docs. But the document regime: trans traveler's passport from home country — wait. Rule 1: visitor uses home passport. If the visitor is foreign, the passport marker rules (US passports) apply to US residents, not foreign visitors. But the entry screening cable (Feb 24, 2025) instructs officers to refuse cases where document discrepancy casts doubt on sex — that applies to visa applicants and entrants, i.e., travelers. Also fraud/lifetime ineligibility. So the federal exposure to a foreign trans visitor: visa refusal, secondary screening, potential fraud finding, and if detained, immigration custody conditions including documented abuse of trans detainees. Also multiple foreign governments issued travel advisories for trans people.

Also federal facility rule: barred from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with identity — applies to airports? government buildings. State-level: no facility ban, protections.

Immigration custody abuse documented — that's state-tolerated/targeting tier 2, but only for those detained, not universal. The document discrepancy → refusal is universal-ish exposure for outed travelers, but severity is denial of entry (severity 3), not imprisonment. Combined with documented custody abuse raising severity if detained.

Working: also trans-specific healthcare shield at state level protects visitors from ban jurisdictions.

I'd place around 0.50-0.58. The parent regime has serious exposures: visa refusals, fraud lifetime bar, custody abuse, federal facility exclusion, hostile federal climate, foreign advisories. The division is strongly protective: public accommodations, hate crime law, shield law, no bathroom ban.

Anchors: 0.55-B (secondary screening, refused admission, administrative, no criminal) — quite close for the border stage. But documented immigration custody abuse is worse than 0.55 anchors. 0.65 anchors show remedies working with brief detention and apology — here remedies at state level work but federal is hostile and custody abuse documented. 0.45-A: routine exposure at checkpoints, detention, denial of care, inconsistent — hmm.

The federal document/entry regime is a universal exposure at the border (every trans traveler with mismatched documents faces doubt → refusal), severity: denial of entry + possible fraud finding; and detention exposure with documented abuse (severity 4). Combined with a state that protects daily life. I'd say ~0.50-0.55.

Consider adult with minor: federal EO on minor care; state protects care; shield law protects visitors from ban jurisdictions — but whether non-resident minors covered is not specified (not_documented). Schools EO investigating — applies federally funded schools, could reach a visiting minor in school settings? Not really a tourist issue.

Let me settle at 0.52.

Factor matrix entries, concise.

Anchor checks: 0.35-A (Vellandra — entry register/exclusion), 0.55-B (Kestrel Isles secondary screening/refused admission), 0.75-C (Meridia trained border officers, brief detention with remedies).

Comparison: higher than 0.35-A (no routine universal exclusion register, no no-remedy agency; strong state protections in daily life); similar-to-slightly-below 0.55-B (documented custody abuse and fraud-referral threat exceed routine administrative screening); below 0.75-C (no trained respectful inspection, documented custody abuse, hostile federal posture).

Rating: 0.52.
